<reason>Both sides were sharp, disciplined, and stayed on the motion, but B built the cleaner decision rule and defended it under pressure. B's core reframe — ownership does not change hydrology, it changes who bears the burden of uncertainty and who must prove harm before acting — directly absorbed A's best line ("a change of title is not a change of water"). B's "same pump, opposite default" answer (nobody sues a city for declining to renew a short supply contract, whereas revoking a vested permit means building a litigation-proof causation record) gave a concrete reason the ban does work A's cap cannot, and B pre-empted A's fallback by asking who drafts the perfect revocable permit, before the drought, against a counterparty whose lawyers negotiate that one clause for a living. B also defused two of A's openings cleanly and honestly: the trade ban is scoped to municipal/aquifer rights for bottling, so the farmer-payment market is untouched; and bottling under public contract continues, so Flint, disaster pallets and grey markets fall away. A extracted a genuine concession there — extraction continues from the same spring — and pressed it well, but B owned that concession and made it the whole clash ("cap the basin, but own the water first"), which A never squarely overcame beyond repeating that paper moves no gallons. A's strongest unanswered point was that the ownership ban seizes springs and groundwater under private parcels; B ignored it, but A never weighed it heavily enough to outweigh B's enforcement story. B also won the pressure exchange on trade: asked to name the actual transaction where a bottler buys aquifer rights and retires farm withdrawals, A supplied only a hypothetical mechanism and then a confusing "they have to be allowed to purchase it," letting B's "a market that exists in theory and not in the basin" stand.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's answer to A's Q1 ("name the well a title ban saves"): the well where the answer must be "no" in year twelve — under a permit that "no" is a taking claim requiring proven causation, under public title it is simply declining to renew. This converted A's "deed vs hydrology" slogan into a question about enforcement defaults, which A only partly answered by asserting a supply contract is a property interest with the serial numbers filed off.</best_rebuttal>
